newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican storm leaves 4,500 homeless - television.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican storm leaves 4,500 homeless - television.

text.p: More than 4,500 people have been left homeless by violent storms on South Africa's southern tip around Cape Town, national television said on Friday.
Local political leaders called on President Nelson Mandela to declare an emergency in some parts of the province of the Western Cape, hit by high winds and rain this week.
Most of the people left homeless are from shanty towns around the city where roofs were blown off and homes flooded.
The television warned of continued high winds combined with rain overnight. It also said sea swells of up to eight metres high were expected.
But weathermen dismissed as "nonsense" fears in Cape Town that a major winter storm of hurricane strength was about to break.

"It's nonsense," a weather office spokesman told Reuters. "There's no cyclone, no hurricane. We're just going to have heavy rain and winds of around 60 to 70 km an hour, the same as we've been having the last few days."
He said no undue disruption was expected at Cape Town's international airport.

Radio stations said factories and offices throughout the city had sent staff home early on Friday in the belief that an exceptionally strong storm would break between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., making travel hazardous.
Over the last week unusually high tides and strong winds have sent surf crashing through the plate-glass patio doors of luxury sea-front homes in the Cape Town area.
Cape Town port captain John Woodend said work had been sporadically disrupted all week.
At Saldanha port further up the West coast, port captain Dave Duncan said an oil tanker, the Stena Continent, had been anchored outside the port since Thursday.
"The prognosis for it coming in does not look good, but it is probably better off where it is than experiencing problems in port," he said.
The tanker is carrying oil for the Caltex Oil (SA) (Pty) Ltd refinery in Cape Town.
Duncan said an ore carrier waiting to load ore from Iscor Ltd's Sishen mine was also at anchor in the bay, sitting out the storm.
He said mussel rafts operated by Lusitania and Sea Harvest had been damaged. "The fishermen have abandoned all fishing now," he said.
